title: One Big Beautiful Bill Act
official_title: To provide for reconciliation pursuant to title II of H. Con. Res. 14.
likelihoodReason: This bill was enacted as Public Law 119-21. It moved through the budget reconciliation process referenced in its title, which allowed Senate passage by a simple majority rather than the usual 60 votes.
summary: This is a 2025 budget reconciliation law that makes the 2017 individual tax cuts permanent, adds new temporary deductions for tips, overtime, car-loan interest, and seniors, and restricts Medicaid and SNAP. It also appropriates tens of billions for border enforcement and defense, expands energy leasing, and raises the federal debt limit by $5 trillion.
brief: A budget reconciliation law that makes the 2017 tax cuts permanent, restricts Medicaid and SNAP, funds border enforcement, and raises the debt limit by $5 trillion.

top_lines.headline: Permanent Individual Tax Changes
subs: Makes the 2017 individual tax rates and standard deduction permanent
Raises the child tax credit to $2,200 per child
Raises the state and local tax (SALT) deduction cap to $40,000 through 2029

top_lines.headline: New Temporary Deductions
subs: No tax on up to $25,000 of tips through 2028
No tax on up to $12,500 of overtime ($25,000 joint) through 2028
New $6,000 senior deduction and a car-loan interest deduction, both through 2028

top_lines.headline: Medicaid and SNAP Restrictions
subs: Requires states to impose Medicaid community-engagement (work) requirements
Expands SNAP work requirements and shifts benefit costs to states
Restricts Medicaid and SNAP eligibility for certain noncitizens

top_lines.headline: Border and Immigration Enforcement
subs: New immigration application, asylum, and parole fees

top_lines.headline: Energy, Defense, and Debt Limit
subs: Expands onshore, offshore, Alaska, and coal leasing and repeals clean-energy provisions
Adds Department of Defense resources for shipbuilding, munitions, and missile defense
Raises the federal debt limit by $5 trillion

sections.label: Title I - Agriculture, Nutrition, and Forestry

items.main: Expands SNAP work requirements for able-bodied adults and requires states to pay a share of benefit costs based on their payment error rate.
items.detail: States with a payment error rate under 6 percent keep a 100 percent federal share, while higher error rates lower the federal share to as little as 85 percent, raising the state share to 15 percent. The title also restricts SNAP eligibility for certain noncitizens and updates commodity reference prices, crop insurance, and dairy and sugar programs.

items.main: Provides additional Department of Defense resources across shipbuilding, munitions, nuclear forces, air and missile defense, and border support.
items.detail: Separate sections fund enhancements to the defense industrial base, low-cost weapons, air superiority, nuclear forces, and Department of Defense border support and counter-narcotics activities, along with authorized military construction projects.

sections.label: Titles III-IV - Banking, Housing, Commerce, and Transportation

items.main: Caps Consumer Financial Protection Bureau funding, rescinds certain program funds, and funds transportation and space programs.
items.detail: Title III caps the Consumer Financial Protection Bureau's funding and rescinds green retrofit program funds. Title IV funds Coast Guard readiness, air traffic control improvements, spectrum auctions, and Mars and Artemis missions, and rescinds certain other amounts.

sections.label: Titles V-VI - Energy, Natural Resources, and Environment

items.main: Expands federal oil, gas, and coal leasing and repeals or rescinds clean-energy and environmental provisions.
items.detail: The energy title reinstates and expands onshore, offshore, Alaska, and National Petroleum Reserve leasing, restarts coal leasing, addresses the Strategic Petroleum Reserve, and creates an Energy Dominance Financing program. It also repeals and rescinds a range of prior clean-energy and environmental appropriations.

sections.label: Title VII - Finance (Tax, Health, and Debt Limit)

items.main: Makes the 2017 individual tax cuts permanent, adds temporary deductions for tips, overtime, car-loan interest, and seniors, and raises the SALT cap to $40,000.
items.detail: The permanent changes include the reduced rates, increased standard deduction, and a $2,200 child tax credit. The tips ($25,000 cap), overtime ($12,500, or $25,000 joint), car-loan interest ($10,000 cap), and senior ($6,000) deductions all end after December 31, 2028, and the SALT cap reverts to $10,000 after 2029.

items.main: Restricts Medicaid and Affordable Care Act (ACA) subsidies and raises the federal debt limit by $5 trillion.
items.detail: The health subtitle requires states to establish Medicaid community-engagement requirements, limits provider taxes and state directed payments, restricts eligibility for certain noncitizens, tightens ACA premium tax credit eligibility, and creates a Rural Health Transformation Program. A separate subtitle increases the public debt limit by $5 trillion.

sections.label: Title VIII - Health, Education, Labor, and Pensions (Student Aid)

items.main: Overhauls federal student loan limits, repayment, and Pell Grants and adds accountability based on earnings outcomes.
items.detail: The title changes student loan borrowing limits and repayment terms, modifies Pell Grant rules, and makes programs ineligible for aid based on low earning outcomes of graduates.

sections.label: Titles IX-X - Border Enforcement, Immigration, and Judiciary

items.main: Appropriates $46.55B for the border wall and infrastructure and $45B for immigration detention, and creates new immigration fees.
items.detail: It also funds additional U.S. Customs and Border Protection personnel and technology and appropriates funds for U.S. Immigration and Customs Enforcement, the Department of Homeland Security, and the Department of Justice. New fees apply to asylum, parole, employment authorization, and other immigration applications, and a separate subtitle extends and expands the Radiation Exposure Compensation program.

underreported.summary: The new deductions for tips, overtime, car-loan interest, and seniors all terminate after December 31, 2028, while the reduced rates and standard deduction are made permanent.
underreported.why_unreported: The most-publicized new deductions are temporary through 2028, a distinction not apparent from the headline tax-relief framing.

underreported.section: Title X, Subtitle A - Immigration Fees
underreported.summary: Creates a broad set of new fees on immigration applications, including asylum, parole, employment authorization, temporary protected status, and visa integrity fees.
underreported.why_unreported: Beyond enforcement spending, the law imposes a wide new fee regime across immigration applications.

underreported.section: Title X, Subtitle C - Radiation Exposure Compensation
underreported.summary: Extends and expands the Radiation Exposure Compensation program to cover atmospheric testing, uranium mining, and Manhattan Project waste claims.
underreported.why_unreported: A radiation-victim compensation program is carried within the judiciary title of a budget reconciliation law.

gaps: The law makes the 2017 rate cuts permanent but lets its new tips, overtime, car-loan, and senior deductions expire after 2028 without specifying what follows.
The law raises the SALT cap to $40,000 for 2025, then reverts it to $10,000 after 2029, leaving the later cliff unaddressed.
The law requires states to establish Medicaid community-engagement requirements but leaves the timing, exemptions, and verification largely to the states and the Secretary.
The law appropriates $46.55B for border infrastructure and $45B for detention but does not tie those amounts to staffing or capacity targets in its own terms.

featured_quotes.name: Ms. Foxx
featured_quotes.text: The question before the House is: Should the House now consider House Resolution 566? Though the resolution waives all points of order against consideration of the motion to concur in the Senate amendment to H.R. 1, the Committee on Rules is not aware of any violation of the Unfunded Mandates Reform Act, nor has the Congressional Budget Office identified any violation of the act. The reason for this motion is plain and obvious.

featured_quotes.name: Mr. McGovern
featured_quotes.text: We have a letter from the Congressional Budget Office confirming that there are unfunded mandates in this bill.

featured_quotes.name: Ms. Brown
featured_quotes.text: For the first time in history, this bill would force States to pay for part of SNAP benefits, and it would require States to increase their share of administrative costs. This is an unfunded mandate, plain and simple. Let's be clear. The costs are staggering, the consequences are devastating, and the cruelty is deeply disturbing. This policy punishes those who can least afford it: seniors on a fixed income, veterans, and families already forced to choose between gas and groceries. States will be stuck in a corner.

featured_quotes.name: Mr. Langworthy
featured_quotes.text: The stakes for the American people could not be higher. We are rapidly approaching a fiscal cliff. If we do nothing, the Trump tax cuts, the most progrowth tax reforms in generations, will expire. That means higher taxes on nearly every American. That means a gutted child tax credit. That means small businesses will lose the tools they need to survive and to thrive. That means less take-home pay for working families that have already been crushed by the Biden-era inflation. This isn't some hypothetical scenario.

featured_quotes.name: Mr. Thompson
featured_quotes.text: Mr. Speaker, Republicans are openly bragging about how the bill kicks children and the elderly off Medicaid, nutritional assistance, and more, all to pay for another tax break for wealthy Republican donors. My Republican colleagues are not talking about the trillions and trillions of dollars their political giveaway is going to cost. In fact, Mr. Speaker, Vice President Vance has said historic levels of Homeland Security funding in the bill sweetens the deal for the devil.

featured_quotes.name: Mr. Alford
featured_quotes.text: Today, Mr. Speaker, we face a watershed moment for the American people. This Republican majority was given a clear mandate by the American people, which is the America First agenda. This bill is our opportunity to deliver on that agenda. H.R. 1 stops the largest tax increase in U.S. history, while providing the largest tax cut for working-and middle-class families ever, with no tax on tips, no tax on overtime, and tax breaks for seniors.

added: Temporary deductions for tips ($25,000), overtime ($12,500 or $25,000 joint), car-loan interest ($10,000), and seniors ($6,000), all ending after 2028
A Medicaid community-engagement (work) requirement and a Rural Health Transformation Program
$46.55B for border wall and infrastructure and $45B for immigration detention
New immigration application, asylum, and parole fees
modified: The 2017 individual tax rates and increased standard deduction made permanent
The child tax credit raised to $2,200 per child
The SALT deduction cap raised to $40,000 for 2025, reverting to $10,000 after 2029
SNAP work requirements expanded, with benefit-cost sharing shifted to states by payment error rate
removed: Repeals and rescissions of prior clean-energy and environmental provisions across several titles
A cap on Consumer Financial Protection Bureau funding
